forefront: There is no institution here, so there is nothing to hold responsible — and caste is culture, not religion.
healthy: Hinduism has ~1.1–1.2 billion adherents, overwhelmingly in India and Nepal.
money: Guru organizations draw on donation empires, ashram real estate, branded products and diaspora funding.
reach: Contemporary nationalist pressure on textbooks, films, scholars, and journalists narrows public discussion of religious history.
techniques: Thirty named techniques from domestic-abuse and social-psychology research, applied to institutions, in the eight stages of the cycle.
loops: The seven loops below show how the practices connect, so that each step makes the next one easier and the last step feeds the first.
say-do: The last time was the convictions of two mass-following gurus, with their organizations continuing and their political patrons silent.
ledger: Dalits and lower-caste communities pay, bearing the tradition's oldest and largest structural harm.
who-gets-hurt: The table names who carries the most, how they carry it, and what makes it worse.
tiers: The table sets out what each role does, what it sees, what it is asked to do and where it could refuse.
voices: Bindu Ammini later had to leave Kerala after attacks.
questions: If karma explains a Dalit child's poverty, explain what it says about the family that inherited the land.
leaving: Caste discrimination at work is covered by existing law in some places and expressly in Seattle.
